recommendation.mainDriver: Commercial-aircraft delivery ramp with pricing discipline
recommendation.mainRisk: Engine shortages delay output and cash conversion
prose: HOLD. The 12-month target price is EUR 211.4, implying 2.0% upside from the current price of EUR 207.30.

The current EUR 207.3 share price already assumes Airbus executes most of the visible production ramp. The market-implied model reaches a 9.7% EBIT margin in 2029, versus 11.5% in the maintained model. It still assumes revenue rises from EUR 80.9bn in 2026 to EUR 108.1bn in 2029. Airbus has 9,222 commercial aircraft in backlog and targets approximately 870 deliveries in 2026, but delivered only 351 in the first half. Second-half delivery cadence therefore matters more than demand discovery.

The evidence supports the industrial opportunity, but not a smooth execution path. Airbus targets more than 1,100 annual deliveries by 2029, 75 A320-family aircraft per month by end-2027 and 12 A350s per month in 2028. Pratt & Whitney engine commitments have led to a formal contractual dispute, CFM declined incremental 2026 volumes, and cabin-equipment constraints have affected A350 output. Inventory rose to EUR 41.7bn in 2025, while the model shows negative FCFF in 2027. Delivery growth without supply-chain coordination can consume, rather than release, value.

The strongest case against HOLD is that Airbus combines a record backlog, scarce certified production slots and a weakened large-aircraft competitor. This could allow pricing and mix to outperform the model, supporting a premium closer to Saab-like defence multiples or Airbus's own 16.51x normalised EV/EBITDA history. The rating remains HOLD because Commercial Aircraft accounts for roughly four-fifths of estimated current enterprise value, 2026 P/E is 27.76x and free-cash-flow conversion remains volatile.

The rating would move to BUY if engine receipts, completed-aircraft handovers and advances support a credible path to at least EUR 16bn of 2029 EBITDA without a comparable inventory build. It would move to SELL if the 75-per-month narrowbody target slips beyond 2027, Space Systems records another material fixed-price charge, or A350F certification moves into 2028 while launch customers reduce commitments.

thesisReasons.title: Backlog converts scarcity into pricing power
thesisReasons.body: The 9,222-aircraft backlog represents more than ten years of output at 2026 guidance. It protects demand visibility and shifts the key question from order capture to physical delivery, escalation clauses and mix.

thesisReasons.title: The earnings ramp is operationally plausible
thesisReasons.body: The maintained model reaches EUR 12.4bn of EBIT in 2029, consistent with management's EUR 12–13bn Adjusted EBIT ambition. This requires narrowbody and A350 production rates to be achieved without abnormal concessions.

thesisReasons.title: Cash conversion is the unresolved constraint
thesisReasons.body: Model FCFF is EUR 3.8bn in 2026, negative in 2027 and only EUR 0.4bn in 2028. Working capital and investment absorb the increase in accounting profit, so the valuation cannot rely on near-term FCF yield.

recommendation.thesisBreaker: A combined delivery-rate miss, price dilution and renewed Space Systems charges would invalidate the margin and cash-conversion path.

sharePrice.context: The evidence supports a rerating as deliveries, EBIT and the defence order environment improved, but it does not explain every share-price move. The July 2026 mid-term outlook, EUR 5bn buyback and reaffirmed production targets support confidence. Engine availability, inventory and weak near-term FCFF limit it. The EUR 232 target offers limited execution-adjusted upside from EUR 207.3.

valuePools.name: Commercial Aircraft and Services
deepDive: ### The prize is lower airline costs, not the aircraft-market label

The economic prize is the airline operating cost that new aircraft can remove, rather than the annual value of delivered airframes. IATA put global airline fuel spending at USD 350bn for 2026. Newer A320neo and A321neo aircraft reduce fuel burn and emissions by approximately 24% per seat versus prior generations. Applying this efficiency to one-quarter of the fuel bill gives a theoretical annual saving pool of USD 21bn: USD 350bn multiplied by 25% of fleet spend multiplied by 24%. Airbus does not capture all of that saving, but it supports aircraft pricing, lease rates and replacement demand. The commercial-aircraft market is smaller and inconsistently defined. Fortune Business Insights estimates USD 131.17bn for 2026, while other researchers cite USD 178.5bn to USD 282.8bn because they include different aircraft and service categories. The valuation uses delivered-aircraft economics and services, not the largest market-research estimate.

The required Commercial Aircraft contribution is demanding but measurable. The model requires EUR 8.5bn of EBIT in 2028, roughly 75% of group EBIT and nearly double FY2025 reported EBIT. If Commercial Aircraft total sales reach approximately EUR 69bn in 2028, the implied EBIT margin is 12.3%. This is 360 basis points above the FY2025 reported margin of 8.7%, calculated as EUR 4.555bn divided by EUR 52.577bn of total segment sales. The bridge does not require a major market-share gain. It requires Airbus to convert its existing order book into roughly 1,000 annual deliveries, with higher A321 and widebody mix, escalation and services revenue, while reducing disruption per aircraft.
### Share is sufficient; delivery conversion is the constraint

Airbus delivered 793 commercial aircraft in 2025, versus Boeing's 600, giving Airbus a 56.9% share of their combined deliveries. Through July 2026, Airbus remained ahead, with third-party data placing its share at 53.2% and Boeing at 46.8%. Airbus and Boeing still control more than 90% of the global single-aisle market. COMAC delivered only 29 aircraft in 2025, and its EASA validation is not expected until 2028–2031. Embraer delivered 66 commercial aircraft in 2025 but mainly serves smaller-capacity categories. Airbus does not need major share gains to meet the bridge. Retaining approximately half of the large-aircraft duopoly while industry output expands is sufficient.

The backlog gives unusually strong demand visibility. Airbus reported 9,222 commercial aircraft at 30 June 2026, versus 793 deliveries in 2025 and guidance for approximately 870 in 2026. Dividing backlog by guidance implies 10.6 years of output before cancellations, substitutions and future orders. This does not guarantee revenue because customer credit, escalation, deposits and delivery timing differ. It does, however, give Airbus scope to protect slot value. Repeated contractual delays or specification changes could shift negotiating leverage back to customers.

- Airbus: 793 commercial deliveries in 2025; 9,222-aircraft backlog at 30 June 2026; approximately 870 deliveries targeted for 2026.
- Boeing: 600 commercial deliveries in 2025; 46.8% of combined Airbus-Boeing deliveries through July 2026.
- Embraer: 66 commercial deliveries in 2025, concentrated below Airbus's core large-aircraft categories.
- COMAC: 29 deliveries in 2025; EASA validation estimated for 2028–2031.
### The production bridge works only if engines arrive

The required volume path is clear. Airbus delivered 351 aircraft in the first half of 2026, so achieving 870 requires 519 in the second half, 48% more than the first-half total. A stronger second half is normal because of seasonality and year-end handovers, but the arithmetic leaves little room for coordinated shortages. Management then targets more than 1,100 deliveries by 2029, a 26% increase from 2026 guidance and a 39% increase from 2025 output. The A320-family target is 75 per month by end-2027. A350 production is targeted at 12 per month in 2028, and A220 production at 13 per month in 2028.

Engines are the main dependency. An airframe completed without engines ties up inventory, supplier cash and customer advances without becoming a delivery. Airbus began a formal process to enforce contractual rights against Pratt & Whitney after it did not commit required 2026 engine volumes. CFM also capped LEAP-1A commitments at previously agreed levels while prioritising the installed fleet. The apparent conflict around rate 75 is timing-related: Airbus retains the end-2027 target, while the chief executive warned that insufficient Pratt guarantees could cause it to be missed. The base valuation gives weight to the official target, but not certainty. The 17.0x multiple is above the 2028 peer EV/EBIT median because the backlog is stronger, while the profit input remains below a smooth ramp.

Spirit AeroSystems integration reduces one external dependency but increases Airbus's execution responsibility. Airbus completed the acquisition of key Spirit industrial assets in December 2025 and received USD 439m of compensation under the transfer agreement. Bringing aerostructure sites closer to Airbus can improve sequencing and investment control, particularly for A220 and A350 work packages. It does not resolve engine, seat, lavatory, landing-gear or lower-tier capacity constraints. The Belfast A220 wing-facility extension of 6,221 square metres shows that Airbus is adding capacity, but returns depend on utilisation rather than floor area.
### Pricing and mix have to do more than unit growth

A narrowbody transaction-price range of USD 50–65m is well below an indicative USD 132.5m A321neo list price. Published list prices are therefore not a usable revenue model. Airbus's FY2025 commercial total sales of EUR 52.577bn divided by 793 deliveries equals EUR 66.3m per delivery, but this includes widebodies, services and other programme revenue and is not an aircraft price. A reasonable 2028 bridge is approximately 1,000 deliveries multiplied by an average recognised aircraft-and-service contribution of EUR 64–67m, plus EUR 3–5bn of additional service and programme revenue, producing EUR 67–72bn. The base uses the middle of that range.

Mix can add more value than headline delivery growth. A321 variants have greater value than smaller A320-family aircraft. A350 deliveries generate more revenue per unit but expose Airbus to cabin-equipment and engine bottlenecks. The A321XLR's Pratt & Whitney-powered version obtained EASA type certification in February 2025, expanding the addressable route set without requiring airlines to buy a widebody. Boeing's 777X certification is expected in 2027, while COMAC lacks near-term broad Western validation. This leaves Airbus with a useful certified-product window. Pricing power would be overstated if Airbus compensates customers heavily for late delivery or weakens escalation to retain orders.
### Services improve durability but cannot offset a failed ramp

Services include maintenance, training, upgrades, flight operations support and digital tools across the installed fleet. Global MRO revenue was estimated at USD 104bn in 2024, and aircraft downtime can exceed USD 100,000 per day for large operators. These economics support recurring demand and make availability, spares and predictive maintenance valuable. Services should require less working capital than new-aircraft production and can reduce programme cyclicality. However, Airbus does not disclose a separate Commercial Aircraft services margin in the supplied evidence. The model therefore does not assign a standalone premium franchise value.

The installed base also creates obligations. Engine maintenance, labour and materials costs for large US airlines increased 68% from 2019 to 2025. This can accelerate demand for efficient aircraft, but can also lead engine makers to prioritise in-service support over production engines. Airbus benefits when older fleets become more expensive to operate, but suffers when the same maintenance burden diverts supplier capacity. The customer saving is real, but Airbus captures it only after handing over a complete, certified aircraft.
### Cash conversion is the decisive evidence test

The consolidated model shows revenue rising from EUR 80.929bn in 2026 to EUR 101.401bn in 2028. EBIT rises from EUR 7.648bn to EUR 11.272bn. Yet FCFF is only EUR 3.764bn in 2026, negative EUR 187m in 2027 and EUR 439m in 2028. Forecast working-capital movements of EUR 4.330bn and EUR 4.943bn in 2027 and 2028 absorb much of the earnings increase. This is consistent with a ramp that requires inventory, supplier support and production assets before delivery. It is also the clearest reason not to apply an unqualified premium for limited capacity.

FY2025 already provided a warning. Inventories rose to EUR 41.676bn from EUR 31.046bn, while the Valuatum cash-flow definition showed FCFF of negative EUR 8.300bn and operating cash flow of EUR 3.020bn. A separate company-adjusted FCF definition reported EUR 4.6bn, showing how materially cash measures differ with the treatment of customer financing, acquisitions and other adjustments. This report uses the authoritative Valuatum model for valuation consistency. The investment case improves if inventory converts into deliveries and advances. It weakens if inventory growth becomes structural.
### Valuation and break conditions

The target bridge values Commercial Aircraft at EUR 144.5bn of target EV, using EUR 8.5bn of modelled 2028 EBIT and a 17.0x multiple. This is below Airbus's 2026 group EV/EBIT multiple of 21.59x and the 2025 historical 30.43x. It is only slightly above the 2028 peer median of 17.8x on an EBIT basis, after allowing for the division's backlog and duopoly. The multiple is not the main source of upside. The EBIT build is. A 10% miss in divisional EBIT removes EUR 14.45bn of EV, or approximately EUR 18.3 per share before secondary cash effects.

Value can break in stages rather than through one demand shock. First, engine receipts or cabin equipment delay rate 75 and increase completed-aircraft inventory. Second, customer compensation and expediting costs prevent margin expansion despite deliveries. Third, working capital does not unwind, so accounting EBIT does not convert into cash and net debt rises above the model's EUR 6.9bn 2028 level. The main leading indicators are monthly deliveries, engine-powered gliders awaiting completion, inventory growth relative to sales and customer-advance movements. A sustained path to more than 1,100 annual deliveries with 12% divisional EBIT margins would support a value above the base bridge.

valuePools.name: Helicopters
deepDive: ### The prize is mission availability in remote, emergency and defence operations

Helicopters compete for spending that would otherwise go to ground logistics, fixed infrastructure, slower emergency response and military mobility. No single global estimate of this displaced spending is available. The closest direct measure is the helicopter-based transportation market at USD 6.56bn in 2026, while the labelled helicopter market is larger. Global Market Insights estimates USD 36.3bn for 2026 and Fortune Business Insights estimates USD 50.02bn, reflecting different treatment of military platforms, services and components. The valuation uses Airbus's reported sales, deliveries and service mix rather than either headline estimate. North America represented an estimated 34.18% of the 2025 market, making US civil and military access important.

The required contribution is modest relative to Airbus's current position. Airbus Helicopters generated EUR 8.972bn of total segment sales and EUR 953m of reported EBIT in 2025, a 10.6% margin. The bridge requires EUR 1.2bn of EBIT in 2028. At a 12% margin, this requires EUR 10bn of sales, only 11% above FY2025. At the FY2025 margin, it would require EUR 11.3bn. The base assumes better mix and services alongside volume, not a transformation in market share.
### Airbus leads civil bookings and is increasing military exposure

Airbus reported 51% of global civil and parapublic helicopter unit bookings in 2025 and 28% of military bookings. These are booking shares, not revenue or installed-fleet shares, but they indicate competitive strength. Airbus delivered 392 helicopters in 2025, compared with Leonardo's reported 182 units and Bell's 169 commercial helicopters. Sikorsky delivered 101 Black Hawk and Seahawk units, illustrating the higher revenue and mission content possible in military heavy platforms despite lower unit volumes.

Competitor data need careful interpretation. Secondary sources report Leonardo's 2025 Helicopters revenue at both EUR 5.25bn and EUR 5.83bn. This report uses EUR 5.83bn because it is paired with EUR 523m of EBITA and appears to cover the full division, while retaining the lower figure as a scope warning. Leonardo also claims approximately 70% share in the 8.5-tonne category and 60% of offshore, search-and-rescue and wind-support deliveries during 2021–2025. Robinson's 85–90% share of certified piston production does not conflict with its 78% active-fleet share because the denominators differ. These niches show that Airbus's 51% civil booking share does not imply leadership in every weight class.

- Airbus Helicopters: 392 deliveries and 51% civil/parapublic booking share in 2025; military booking share reached 28%.
- Leonardo Helicopters: 182 deliveries in 2025; revenue reported at EUR 5.25–5.83bn depending on source scope.
- Bell: 169 commercial deliveries and USD 4.28bn revenue in 2025; segment margin was 8.5%.
- Sikorsky: 101 Black Hawk and Seahawk deliveries in 2025, concentrated in higher-value military missions.
### Mix is more important than the number of airframes

A civil H135 base price was approximately USD 6.15m in 2026. The August 2026 US Army order for ten UH-72B Lakotas was worth USD 115.4m, or USD 11.54m per aircraft including the contractual package. Dividing FY2025 total sales by 392 deliveries gives EUR 22.9m per delivered helicopter, but this includes military platforms, support, spare parts, training and revenue unrelated to current-period deliveries. It therefore indicates mix and installed-base value, not a unit price. The route to EUR 1.2bn of EBIT is greater military and service mix, not simply more light-civil units.

Military demand provides the clearest support for mix. Airbus's military booking share rose to 28% in 2025, and the UH-72B award shows continued access to the US Army. European rearmament also supports procurement, although helicopter budgets compete with fixed-wing aircraft, missiles, drones and land systems. Military contracts can offer long support tails and higher mission-system content. However, fixed-price development or local-content obligations can transfer risk to the manufacturer. The bridge assumes mature-platform production and support, not a loss-making clean-sheet programme.

Civil demand remains important because it broadens the installed base and aftermarket. GAMA reported 938 civilian helicopter deliveries worth USD 4.7bn in 2025, implying an industry average of about USD 5.0m per unit across piston and turbine categories. Airbus products are weighted toward more expensive turbine and twin-engine platforms, so unit share understates its revenue opportunity. Civil fleet flight hours increased 3.9% in the first half of 2026, supporting parts consumption and maintenance. Offshore and corporate demand can still be cyclical and interest-rate sensitive.
### Services turn the installed base into recurring revenue

The installed fleet creates demand for mandatory maintenance, parts, training, upgrades and mission-system support. An H145's estimated variable operating cost is USD 1,516 per flight hour, showing that customers focus on availability and mission completion, not acquisition price alone. Airbus can monetise this through support-by-the-hour contracts, spare-parts availability and digital fleet management. Higher flight hours should increase service events, although operators may defer discretionary upgrades when budgets tighten.

Services reduce the importance of annual deliveries. H1 2026 revenue was EUR 3.7bn on 144 deliveries, with EUR 240m of adjusted EBIT. Simply doubling this would produce EUR 7.4bn of revenue and EUR 480m of adjusted EBIT, below FY2025. However, deliveries and support revenue are seasonally weighted, and contract mix changes between halves. The H1 margin of 6.5% cautions against extrapolating the 10.6% FY2025 reported margin without a stronger second half. The valuation therefore uses a 15.0x multiple on 2028 EBIT rather than the Commercial Aircraft premium.
### Competitive niches cap aggregate pricing power

Leonardo is strongest in super-medium, offshore and selected government categories. Sikorsky anchors the Black Hawk family, Bell combines civil products with military growth, and Robinson dominates low-cost piston production. Airbus's broad portfolio spans light twins, medium civil platforms, parapublic missions and military aircraft. This breadth is strategically useful, but lower-value civil deliveries can dilute average economics. The division earns a premium only if military and service growth outpace lower-margin new civil units.

Bell provides a useful profitability reference. Its 2025 segment margin was 8.5%, 210 basis points below Airbus Helicopters' reported 10.6%. Leonardo's reported EUR 523m of EBITA on EUR 5.83bn of revenue implies approximately 9.0%, although EBITA is not the same as Airbus reported EBIT. These comparisons support a low-double-digit Airbus margin but do not show that 14–15% is sustainable. The base case therefore uses 12% at the required sales level.
### Valuation and evidence path

The target bridge values Helicopters at EUR 18.0bn, using EUR 1.2bn of modelled 2028 EBIT and a 15.0x multiple. The multiple exceeds Lockheed Martin's 2028 EV/EBIT of 12.0x and Textron's 10.3x because Airbus Helicopters has stronger civil share and a valuable service franchise. It remains below the Commercial Aircraft multiple because the addressable market is smaller and more fragmented. Relative to EUR 953m of FY2025 reported EBIT, the bridge requires 26% cumulative profit growth over three years. This is achievable if sales rise toward EUR 10bn and margin reaches 12%.

The evidence sequence is clear. First, 2026 deliveries and second-half margin must recover from the H1 cadence. Second, military booking share should remain near or above the reported 28%, with awards converting into production rather than development charges. Third, fleet flight hours and service revenue should grow faster than civil new-aircraft sales. The valuation would rise if service and military mix support EUR 1.35bn of 2028 EBIT. At the same multiple, the additional EUR 150m adds EUR 2.25bn of EV. It would fall if margin remains near Bell's 8.5%, which on EUR 10bn of sales produces only EUR 850m of EBIT and reduces target EV by EUR 5.25bn.
### What breaks the value

The first risk is a mix reversal, with strong light-civil unit volumes but weak military and service contribution. The second is contract quality, particularly if sovereign customers require fixed-price development, local assembly or supplier risk that pricing does not cover. The third is underused installed capacity, visible in lower flight hours and deferred maintenance. The fourth is displacement in profitable niches by Leonardo, Sikorsky or Bell. None alone negates the franchise, but together they would make the 15.0x multiple and EUR 1.2bn EBIT assumption too generous.

valuePools.name: Air Power
deepDive: ### The prize is sovereign aircraft and sustainment spending

Aviation Week projects USD 2.7tn of global military-aircraft and sustainment spending for 2026–2035, or approximately USD 270bn annually. The narrower new-aircraft market is estimated at USD 67.29bn in 2026, while conflicting 2025 estimates range from USD 59.72bn to USD 63.63bn. The valuation uses Airbus programme revenue rather than these market labels. European rearmament could add USD 110bn of aircraft spending over 2025–2032, supporting Airbus's geographic demand mix if procurement becomes funded contracts.

This report models FY2025 Air Power revenue at EUR 7.5bn and EBIT at EUR 450m within reported Defence and Space totals. The split is not company-reported. It allocates EUR 13.335bn of external revenue among Air Power, Space Systems and Connected Intelligence using disclosed programme activity, while reconciling the three divisions to the authoritative segment total. The bridge requires EUR 800m of 2028 EBIT. At an 8% margin, this implies EUR 10bn of revenue; at 10%, EUR 8bn. The base therefore depends more on contract quality and mix than on exceptional sales growth.
### Airbus is strong in transport and tankers, but not fighters

The C295 holds an 80% position in medium tactical transport, while A330 MRTT has approximately 90% of tanker orders outside the United States. The A400M and C295 together represent roughly 10% of the active global military-cargo fleet, versus about 20% for the C-130 family. Lockheed Martin leads the fighter market and benefits from the scale of the F-35. Airbus participates in Eurofighter but does not control all economics or national workshare decisions.

A400M economics remain the main industrial swing factor. Production is stabilised at eight units annually through early 2029, with 140 cumulative aircraft delivered by August 2026. Published unit values vary sharply. General estimates put the aircraft at USD 145–152m, while an Indian procurement estimate cited USD 210m. These figures are not comparable because flyaway, development, support and package content differ. The valuation does not derive programme margin from any single unit figure.

- Airbus: C295 80% tactical-transport position; A330 MRTT roughly 90% of non-US tanker orders; A400M rate eight per year.
- Lockheed Martin: C-130 family about 20% of active cargo fleet; F-35 airframe reference USD 82.4m excluding engines.
- Embraer: C-390 reference price around USD 140m; competing for India's 60-aircraft tender.
- Boeing: C-17 about 6% of active cargo inventory; production line closed.
### Procurement supports growth, but contract terms determine value

Germany approved EUR 3.75bn for 20 Eurofighter Tranche 5 aircraft, and Spain contracted 25 additional Eurofighters for EUR 4.0bn. Spain also ordered 16 C295 maritime aircraft for EUR 1.695bn. Italy's six-aircraft A330 MRTT package was reported at EUR 1.6bn, implying EUR 267m per aircraft including support, versus a separate USD 275m flyaway estimate. These awards demonstrate demand, but also show why package scope must be separated from airframe price.

India's request for proposal for 60 medium transports is valued at approximately USD 10.5–11bn and pits A400M against C-390 and C-130J. A win would extend production visibility beyond the existing European backlog. A loss would reinforce the risk that the Seville line lacks orders after 2028. Airbus's larger payload and strategic capability may support pricing, but its higher acquisition cost can be a disadvantage where customers prioritise tactical missions. The base valuation does not assume an Indian win.

FCAS is an additional uncertainty rather than a base-value driver. One July 2026 report described the fighter project as collapsed, while Airbus said German Team Gen 6 work continued. The most defensible view is that the original industrial structure faces serious political pressure, while some funded collaborative technologies remain active. No material FCAS terminal value is included. A restructured, funded workshare would be upside.
### Valuation and failure path

Air Power is valued at EUR 10.4bn, using EUR 800m of modelled 2028 EBIT and a 13.0x multiple. The multiple is close to Lockheed Martin's 2028 12.0x and below Northrop Grumman's 19.4x. It reflects Airbus's strong transport positions but greater European workshare and fixed-price risk. The key evidence is Defence and Space order intake of EUR 9.3bn in H1 2026 and EUR 17.7bn for 2025, although Air Power-specific backlog is unavailable.

Value falls if A400M production ends without an export bridge, Eurofighter workshare does not convert national awards into Airbus revenue, or fixed-price contracts generate charges. It rises if India selects A400M, MRTT exports continue and the division reaches a sustainable high-single-digit margin. As programme margins are undisclosed, order quality and cash milestones matter more than announced contract value.

valuePools.name: Connected Intelligence
deepDive: ### The prize is the intelligence and mapping workflow

Surveying and mapping services generated an estimated USD 159.5bn in 2025, representing the wider workflow spending that geospatial-intelligence products can partly replace or automate. The narrower GEOINT market is disputed. MarketsandMarkets estimates USD 37.13bn with 11.1% growth, while Fortune Business Insights estimates USD 24.18bn with 8.71% growth. The valuation uses modelled Airbus revenue, not the higher market estimate. North America represented 38.92% of the GEOINT market, highlighting the importance of allied access and classified procurement.

This report models FY2025 Connected Intelligence revenue at EUR 1.835bn and EBIT at EUR 289m, a 15.7% margin. These are derived allocations within Defence and Space, not company-reported subsegment results. The bridge requires EUR 400m of 2028 EBIT. At a 16% margin, this requires EUR 2.5bn of revenue, a EUR 665m increase from the modelled base.
### Airbus has credible positions but no single disclosed market share

Airbus is estimated to lead SATCOM with only 4.8% share, while the top five providers collectively hold 19.3%, indicating a fragmented market. Airbus Defence and Space is ranked second worldwide in GEOINT. Maxar's commercial EO share is reported at 35% for high-resolution imagery and 21.3% for the broader satellite-based EO market. The figures differ because the denominators and periods differ. Planet Labs holds an estimated 47% of the optical-imaging-payload segment in small-satellite EO.

The PAZ-2 commercialisation agreement with Hisdesat expands access to radar imagery, complementing optical data and supporting all-weather monitoring. Secure communications, command-and-control and analytics can generate recurring subscription and service revenue beyond one-time satellite manufacturing. The exact recurring-revenue mix is unavailable. The model therefore applies a premium multiple to profit, rather than a software revenue multiple.
### Sovereignty is both a demand driver and a cost

Airbus decided to move 70 critical digital-design and sales systems from AWS to French provider Scaleway. Sovereign customers increasingly value data location, supply-chain control and trusted access, which can favour a European prime. The migration also creates transition costs, execution risk and potentially less hyperscale flexibility. The full timetable and economics are not disclosed.

The target value is EUR 6.4bn, based on EUR 400m of 2028 EBIT at 16.0x. This multiple is above mature defence primes because recurring data and secure-connectivity revenue can grow faster and require less capital than aircraft production. It remains below high-growth pure software valuations because customer concentration, classified procurement and deployment obligations limit scalability.
### What breaks the value

Value fails if sovereign spending remains project-based rather than recurring, imagery becomes commoditised by lower-cost constellations, or migration and security requirements raise costs faster than prices. It improves if Airbus demonstrates recurring service growth, converts PAZ-2 and other datasets into multi-year subscriptions, and maintains a mid-teens EBIT margin. Separate disclosure of revenue, backlog and recurring revenue would provide the strongest evidence.

valuePools.name: A350F Freighter Programme
deepDive: ### The prize is time-sensitive freight, not ocean shipping

The broad ocean-freight market is estimated at USD 2.02tn in 2026, but A350F addresses only cargo for which speed, reliability, security and network economics justify air transport. The labelled freighter-aircraft market is USD 4.81bn in 2026. The option valuation uses future A350F programme revenue and margin rather than claiming a share of ocean freight. The displaced-spend comparison explains strategic relevance but is too broad for direct valuation.

The programme has 107 firm orders, while the competing Boeing 777-8F has more than 80. Airbus is estimated to have won approximately half of newly launched next-generation widebody-freighter orders, despite Boeing controlling about 90% of the existing large-freighter fleet. Atlas Air became the largest A350F customer with 20 units. Air France-KLM reduced its order to six and Air Lease cancelled seven, showing that schedule credibility affects customer retention.
### Certification is the value gate

The first aircraft was unveiled in August 2026 after completing ground-vibration and maximum-payload tests. Airbus targets first flight around 24 September 2026, EASA certification in Q2 2027 and entry into service in H2 2027. The certification basis derives from the A350-1000 under EASA CS-25 Amendment 27, with approximately 400 flight hours across two test aircraft. FAA approval remains necessary for broad US operation, but an exact FAA timetable is unavailable.

The 4.5-metre electrically actuated main-deck cargo door is the main new structural dependency. Airbus successfully loaded 111 tonnes in ground testing, matching the published maximum payload. The A350F offers 111 tonnes over 4,700 nautical miles. Boeing payload claims range from 112.3 tonnes in technical specifications to 118 tonnes in secondary reporting. This report weights 112.3 tonnes because it is tied to the stated 4,410-nautical-mile range.
### The option legs use explicit scale economics

The conservative success case assumes 30 annual deliveries by 2030 at EUR 150m of recognised programme revenue per aircraft, producing EUR 4.5bn of revenue. At a 6.7% EBITDA margin, EBITDA is EUR 300m. At 10.0x, EV at scale is EUR 3.0bn. The probability is 35%, supported by 107 orders, completed ground tests and the planned September flight. Customer reductions and the compressed certification schedule reduce this probability.

The upside case assumes 50 annual deliveries by 2030 at EUR 150m each, producing EUR 7.5bn of revenue. At an 8.7% EBITDA margin, EBITDA is EUR 650m. At 12.0x, EV at scale is EUR 7.8bn. Its probability is 20%. The remaining 45% failure outcome receives zero standalone option value because certification delay into 2028, customer attrition or insufficient production rates could leave the programme unable to earn its capital cost. Analyst concern about a 2028 EIS and documented cancellations support this failure weighting.
### What changes the option value

A September first flight, completion of the 400-hour campaign and Q2 2027 EASA certification would shift probability from technical completion toward industrial execution. Retention of all 107 orders and evidence of a repeatable production rate would support the upside case. A flight-test interruption, door redesign or FAA delay would reduce both probability and achievable volume. The option is not valued on current revenue because it is pre-revenue and embedded within Commercial Aircraft reporting.

valuePools.name: Space Systems
deepDive: ### The prize is connectivity and orbital infrastructure, not launcher count

Global telecom and pay-TV spending reached an estimated USD 1.551tn in 2025, representing the broad communications pool that satellite connectivity can partly address. The labelled global space economy is disputed. Novaspace estimates USD 626bn for 2025, while the Space Foundation reports USD 686bn and 12% growth. The valuation uses neither headline directly because Airbus's accessible upstream satellite and launcher market is a small subset. European primes held about 10% of global upstream activity but 65% of their accessible market.

This report models Space Systems at EUR 4.0bn of FY2025 revenue and negative EUR 100m of EBIT within Defence and Space. The split is derived, not separately reported. The target assumes EUR 250m of EBIT in 2028, only a 6.25% margin on unchanged revenue. The investment case is therefore about loss containment and normalisation, not high growth in space.
### Legacy fixed-price programmes determine the turnaround

Airbus recorded EUR 1.3bn of Space Systems charges in 2024, including EUR 989m associated with revised OneSat schedule and cost assumptions in H1. These charges outweighed otherwise attractive demand. The Optus 11 situation remains a warning. The ITU rejected an Australian extension request and described use of an untested design as a known operator risk. The remaining provision and compensation exposure are unavailable.

ADAPT created end-to-end accountability across Air Power, Space Systems and Connected Intelligence. Airbus initially described up to 2,500 position reductions by mid-2026, while the implemented plan identified approximately 2,043 positions, mainly in overhead. This report uses the more specific 2,043 implementation figure and treats 2,500 as the earlier ceiling. The EUR 105m FY2025 workforce-adaptation charge is a near-term cost intended to improve accountability.
### Demand is real, but launch and satellite competition is intense

Eutelsat ordered 340 additional low-earth-orbit satellites, taking its Airbus total to 440, with deliveries scheduled from end-2026. Ariane 6 completed its third Amazon Kuiper mission in June 2026, carrying 36 satellites. These milestones support production learning and backlog conversion. SpaceX nevertheless held about 60% of global launches by count in 2025, while Maxar held an estimated 35% of high-resolution commercial Earth observation.

A proposed consolidation with Leonardo and Thales could improve European scale, reduce duplicated development and strengthen procurement leverage. It could also create governance complexity and require political and competition approvals. No consolidation premium is included in the base value. The division earns its EUR 2.5bn target EV only by showing that remaining fixed-price exposure is limited.
### Valuation and break conditions

The bridge uses EUR 250m of 2028 EBIT at 10.0x, producing EUR 2.5bn of target EV. The multiple is deliberately below defence-electronics peers because the recovery has not yet been proven through cash generation. Management commentary that the rebound was ahead of internal expectations is encouraging, but does not replace programme-level disclosure.

A further charge above EUR 500m would consume two years of modelled EBIT and undermine the turnaround. Conversely, delivery of the OneWeb satellites, stable OneSat milestones and positive divisional EBIT would support a 12–14x multiple. The key evidence is not order intake but provision movement, milestone acceptance and cash collection.

However, the broad 4,632-company ROE/P/BV curve implies only 2.7x book and EUR 119 per share, versus EUR 207.3. The current 4.8x forecast-average P/BV therefore reflects more than accounting returns. It prices backlog durability, advance-funded economics and scarce certified production capacity. The scatter warns against using high ROE alone to support the valuation.

executiveMap: Enterprise value is concentrated in Commercial Aircraft. The key question is whether Airbus can move from approximately 870 deliveries in 2026 to more than 1,100 in 2029 without sacrificing price, margin or cash. The backlog removes near-term demand uncertainty but shifts the investment debate to engines, cabins, completed-aircraft inventory and customer acceptance.

Helicopters is the second profit stream, with a modelled 2028 EBIT margin of 12% supported by military and service mix. Air Power requires EUR 800m of 2028 EBIT from funded, executable contracts. Space Systems must move from modelled losses to EUR 250m without another large fixed-price charge. Connected Intelligence requires approximately EUR 2.5bn of revenue at a 16% margin.

A350F is an option rather than a current profit engine. Its value depends on first flight, Q2 2027 EASA certification, H2 2027 entry into service, retention of 107 orders and an eventual 30–50 aircraft annual rate.
coreAnalysis.analyticalAnchor: Backlog creates value only when a complete aircraft is delivered, accepted and converted into cash. The report therefore views supply-chain coordination, rather than order intake, as Airbus's main valuation constraint.
crossPoolBridge: Commercial Aircraft funds the portfolio but also requires the most ramp capital. Shared procurement and engineering can support Helicopters and Defence and Space. Shortages of engines, aerostructures or specialised labour can also crowd out lower-volume programmes.

Air Power and Connected Intelligence can increase sovereign content per contract. Aircraft platforms create demand for secure communications, surveillance and support. Space Systems provides sensors and connectivity, but fixed-price overruns can absorb group cash and offset this cross-selling value.

A350F reuses the A350 platform, reducing clean-sheet development risk, but competes for widebody engineering and production capacity. Its option value should be added only after recognising funding needs, not treated as free upside.
coreAnalysis.bridgeMechanics: Current EV of EUR 165.140bn is allocated across the six divisions in the value map. The target uses separate target-year EBIT multiples for five profit engines and probability-weighted, discounted EBITDA legs for A350F.
valuationRealityCheck: At EUR 207.3, Airbus trades at 27.76x 2026E earnings, 13.66x EBITDA and 21.59x EBIT. These levels already price a material recovery from the 2025 7.1% EBIT margin.

The reverse valuation allows the group EBIT margin to rise from 8.4% in 2026 to 12.5% terminally. However, it holds 2029 EBIT at EUR 10.491bn, versus EUR 12.418bn in the maintained model. The share price therefore does not assume full management execution.

Peers do not provide a clean answer. Boeing's negative earnings make profit multiples unusable, defence primes lack commercial exposure, and suppliers have different installed-base economics. Airbus's own normalised 16.51x historical EV/EBITDA is a useful upper reference, not an automatic target.

The target's modest premium reflects higher profit-engine EBIT than the market-implied path and only EUR 2.61bn of undiscounted A350F expected EV. Most option value remains unpriced until certification and production evidence improves.
scenarios: Bear: 2028 revenue reaches only EUR 95.0bn and EBITDA EUR 12.35bn, a 13.0% margin. The narrowbody rate of 75 slips, working capital remains elevated, Space Systems records further charges and A350F receives no option value.

Base: 2028 revenue reaches the maintained EUR 101.401bn and EBITDA EUR 14.787bn, a 14.6% margin. Commercial EBIT reaches EUR 8.5bn and Helicopters reaches EUR 1.2bn. The A350F option is probability-weighted between 30- and 50-unit annual-rate legs.

Bull: 2028 revenue reaches EUR 108.0bn and EBITDA EUR 17.7bn, a 16.4% margin. Engine supply supports the production plan, pricing holds, inventory converts, defence mix improves and A350F is valued on its successful high-rate leg. Higher cash generation reduces net debt rather than leaving the base balance sheet unchanged.
coreAnalysis.bottomLine: Airbus has one of the strongest demand positions in industrial Europe, but the stock now depends on production-system reliability rather than the order book. The EUR 232 target recognises credible margin recovery and selective option value, while not applying the full historical premium to an unproven cash-conversion path.

scenarioValuation.keyConditions: The scenario spread is driven mainly by completed-aircraft output, divisional margins and cash release. Bear assumes zero A350F failure value and rising net debt. Base probability-weights the option. Bull uses the successful high-rate A350F case and lower net debt because stronger margins and handovers generate more cash. Each scenario follows the target-price bridge's approach: modelled profit engines plus A350F Freighter Programme at zero in Bear, at the bridge's probability weighting in Base, and at the best single scenario leg with certainty in Bull. The multiple column is therefore implied group EV/EBITDA at that value, not a selected multiple. The code-verified 12-month target of EUR 211.4 sits between Bear and Base, with Bear at EUR 208.9, Base at EUR 211.4 and Bull at EUR 216.5. Its method weights are shown in the Target Price Bridge.

valuation.methodRationale:
SOTP is primary because Commercial Aircraft, helicopters, defence platforms, space turnaround assets, intelligence services and a pre-revenue freighter option have different margins and risk. Profit engines use 2028E EBIT multiples inside the peer and Airbus-history brackets; A350F uses probability-weighted 2030 EBITDA legs. Commercial receives the highest multiple for backlog scarcity, while Space receives the lowest for fixed-price risk. Sensitivity shows that a 10% earnings miss matters more than modest multiple variation.

What the market is pricing.

The five profit engines contribute EUR 182.2bn of target EV before A350F, already above the current EUR 165.140bn EV. At the market price, investors are effectively discounting roughly EUR 17bn from the base profit-engine value and assigning little or no net A350F value. That is equivalent to Commercial Aircraft earning about EUR 7.5bn rather than EUR 8.5bn at 17.0x, with option success near zero.

The market assumes Commercial Aircraft fails to reach the modelled EUR 8.5bn 2028 EBIT level. We assign a different reading: The backlog and production objectives support the EBIT level, but execution risk justifies only a modest target premium; every EUR 850m EBIT change moves EV by EUR 14.45bn. (Airbus, 21 July 2026: rate 75 by end-2027 and 2029 Adjusted EBIT target of EUR 12–13bn.)

The market assumes A350F has negligible standalone value. We assign a different reading: Completed payload and vibration tests plus 107 orders justify EUR 2.61bn of undiscounted expected EV, while the 45% failure remainder recognises certification and customer-retention risk. (Airbus, 3 August 2026; Reuters, 18 August 2026; Airbus programme status, 19 August 2026.)

Two enterprise values, two questions. The division pages allocate today's market enterprise value across the divisions; the target-price bridge states what each is worth on this report's own estimates. For A350F Freighter Programme the two readings are 2.3 billion allocated and 2 billion warranted.
